title: In table 2.2 (p. 26), the two study rows carry each other's labels, in both panels.
published:
After [[pro]]-capital punishment study

After [[anti]]-capital punishment study
corrected:
After [[anti]]-capital punishment study

After [[pro]]-capital punishment study
note: The changed artifact is the two labels alone. Every value is correct, and the rows are in the order the analysis produces them, whose study-content factor runs con before pro and so puts the anti-capital punishment study first. Figure 2.2, printed on the same page from the same variable, shows the con study at 0.0 for proponents and -2.3 for opponents and the pro study at 2.7 and -0.4, which is the table's two rows the other way up. The sentence beneath the figure, reporting that self-assessed change is higher in the pro condition than in the null and higher in the null than in the con, says the same thing again. The "Combined" rows are sums of the two and are unaffected, as is the reading of the table that the surrounding text draws from them.

title: Four sentences in chapter 6 report persistence figures that the chapter's own tables print differently.
published:
Across all 12 studies, the average persistence ratio was about one-third, or 34 percent; that figure is 50 percent in the stronger persistence group and [[20]] percent in the weaker persistence group (see table 6.2).

After ten days treatment effects decay to [[46]] percent (SE = 5 percent) of their original magnitudes.

After thirty days, average persistence declines to [[44]] percent (SE = 6 percent).

For Republicans, persistence after ten days averaged [[57]] percent; this figure was [[43]] percent for Democrats.
corrected:
Across all 12 studies, the average persistence ratio was about one-third, or 34 percent; that figure is 50 percent in the stronger persistence group and [[21]] percent in the weaker persistence group (see table 6.2).

After ten days treatment effects decay to [[48]] percent (SE = 5 percent) of their original magnitudes.

After thirty days, average persistence declines to [[46]] percent (SE = 6 percent).

For Republicans, persistence after ten days averaged [[53]] percent; this figure was [[48]] percent for Democrats.
note: The page 118 sentence is the one that moves furthest, and the two halves fail differently. Its 57 percent is table 6.3's Republican estimate after *thirty* days, read one column across from the ten-day estimate the sentence describes; its 43 percent is no cell of the table at all. The sentence that follows, that the Republican and Democratic estimates are not statistically significantly different, is unaffected and holds on the corrected figures, which are closer together than the published pair. The standard errors on page 117 are left as printed. The ten-day one agrees with table 6.3; the thirty-day one says 6 percent where the table prints 0.05, but the reanalysis returns 6 percent as well, so that figure sits inside the bootstrap's noise in a way none of the five estimates above does. Tables 6.2 and 6.3 are otherwise correct as printed and are not reprinted here.

title: Page 114 attributes a persistence estimate to a sample that is not in the persistence analysis.
published: Curiously, the different replications of the Hiscox (2006) "expert" treatment generated very different persistence estimates: 49 percent on MTurk but 0 percent on [[Lucid]].
corrected: Curiously, the different replications of the Hiscox (2006) "expert" treatment generated very different persistence estimates: 49 percent on MTurk but 0 percent on [[GfK]].
note: Table 6.1 lists twelve panel survey experiments and none of them is fielded on Lucid; the Hiscox rows of table 6.4 are Mechanical Turk and GfK, and table 6.4 gives the zero to GfK. The two percentages are left at the whole numbers the sentence uses because they come from a bootstrap the analysis runs without a seed, and a decimal place would state a precision the estimator does not have.
